title: Everyone’s a Law Company
pub: The Practice (Harvard Law School Center on the Legal Profession), July/August 2019
author: The Practice editorial team

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Corporate buyers: Insourcing and partnerships coexist
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that corporate legal departments gained control over diagnosing and sourcing legal work while law firms remained critical. It materially extends that account by linking buyer-led sourcing changes to the rise of ALSPs and contrasting today’s diversified market with an earlier binary choice between insourcing and law firms.
qs: Law firms, while still critical, were increasingly challenged by corporate legal departments who became both the chief diagnosticians of their companies’ legal problems and the chief purchasing agent responsible for solving them.
Many of these changes have direct connections to the rise of ALSPs in the last 10 to 15 years.

st.t: Provider convergence: Buyers coordinate an unbundled market
st.an: The source accepts the broader-provider, client-solution framing and materially develops it by explaining how legal operations enable informed sourcing, task-by-task provider selection and coordination across law firms, ALSPs and internal teams. It also notes that expanded choice increases the buyer’s navigation burden rather than establishing any provider type as universally superior.
qs: As legal operations professionals have entered the picture to augment in-house legal departments, companies are more conscious of their own processes, more discerning when they need to purchase legal services, and more capable of arriving at truly cost-effective solutions.
With our bottom-up thinking about evaluating activities, it’s really about which company aligns to the activity and outcome we’re trying to achieve.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s work-redesign thesis and materially extends it into procurement and provider architecture. It argues that legal operations should decompose work, match each task and desired outcome to the appropriate provider, and assess quality through objective outputs—showing how selective deployment can reshape workflows and boundaries among in-house teams, law firms and ALSPs. It does not directly address AI capability or verification.
qs: The mindset of clients today, however (and certainly that of many ALSPs), appears to have evolved to put process at the center of their thinking.
With our bottom-up thinking about evaluating activities, it’s really about which company aligns to the activity and outcome we’re trying to achieve.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source directly supports buyer-led workflow unbundling: in-house legal operations evaluate activities, allocate repeatable work among internal teams, law firms and ALSPs, and retain law firms for specialised advice. It also supports output-based quality measurement and coexistence rather than wholesale law-firm displacement, while not addressing the cluster’s later AI-specific training and verification claims.
qs: “The second we were able to understand what the value and the impact of doing that work was and the fact that other providers could do the work, then we said, ‘OK, we can really unbundle this,’” says Stockton.
If we need specialized legal advice, we will always go to a law firm.

kp.k: ALSP growth reflects an established, increasingly mainstream market
kp.d: The editorial presents historical evidence of legal-services restructuring rather than an account of generative AI. It argues that calling ALSPs alternatives obscures their longevity and widespread use. Citing a report published by Thomson Reuters with Georgetown, Oxford Saïd and Acritas, it reports roughly $10.7 billion in ALSP revenues in 2017, compared with roughly $8.4 billion in 2015, an increase of $2.3 billion. It attributes growth to client demands for cost-effectiveness and value, rather than endorsing reported predictions of big law's demise.
qs: Not only are these so-called “alternatives” increasingly used across the legal ecosystem by clients of all sizes and types, but many of today’s major ALSP players have in fact been around for decades.
For example, legal staffing companies Axiom and Legility (formerly Counsel on Call) were both founded in 2000—nearly 20 years ago.

kp.k: In-house counsel and legal operations reshape purchasing
kp.d: The editorial traces corporate clients' increased purchasing authority to the in-house movement beginning in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Legal operations subsequently expanded clients' capacity to manage budgets, vendors and staffing, making ALSPs part of routine sourcing decisions. Booz Allen Hamilton's Kurt Grasinger describes considering the full range of providers as an emerging management expectation, not simply an optional departure from traditional law-firm relationships.
qs: Law firms, while still critical, were increasingly challenged by corporate legal departments who became both the chief diagnosticians of their companies’ legal problems and the chief purchasing agent responsible for solving them.
Now, it’s almost an expectation of management that they consider the full universe of options—including ALSPs—to solve each problem.
Legal operations (also known as “legal ops”) is about building capacity within organizations to think critically about their legal spend from every possible angle.

kp.k: Process analysis enables unbundling beyond e-discovery
kp.d: Fidelity's Jamal Stockton describes e-discovery as the initial entry point for process-focused sourcing, followed by end-to-end examination of legal work from intake to close. His account connects internal workload pressure, measurable service value and the availability of lower-cost providers to unbundling. Reallocating manual intake activities to a more-junior associate on a different track is presented as a way to reduce costs and restore attorneys' capacity, not as evidence of AI displacement.
qs: “For most folks that journey started with e-discovery,” Stockton says.
Over time the approach to rethinking internal processes for legal operations became end to end—from intake to close.
It makes us much more efficient but also lowers our cost and gives our attorneys capacity back to focus on lawyering.

kp.k: Staffing decisions increasingly compare internal shifts and ALSPs
kp.d: Fidelity's Diane Brown describes a staffing committee that examines resource needs rather than automatically adding headcount. Options include internal work redistribution and ALSP engagement, with the choice depending on the underlying need. Fidelity's flexible staffing program can support transitions across practice areas without necessarily hiring permanent employees or relying on law firms.
qs: We no longer have the mindset that adding headcount is always the answer.
Ultimately, we’re trying to determine whether internal shifts in work to give attorneys capacity back is warranted and possible or if an ALSP is the optimal solution.
As the department evolves and strives to be more efficient, ALSPs can help during those transitional phases—avoiding the need to lean on law firms or hire permanent staff.

kp.k: ALSP careers gain legitimacy through flexibility
kp.d: Brown and Grasinger describe changing perceptions of contract lawyers, moving away from assumptions that they lack other options. They identify family circumstances, career experimentation, balance and continued engagement in sophisticated work as reasons for deliberately choosing ALSP careers. These are interview-based observations about career preferences and client perceptions, rather than quantified findings about employment outcomes.
qs: Perceptions have grown quite a bit in terms of recognizing that attorneys are in the contract model for any number of reasons, and it’s not simply because they’re undesirable or incapable.
“A lot of ALSPs have experienced, credentialed lawyers,” says Grasinger, echoing Brown.
They often also have a flexibility model that many find attractive, both on the client side and on the employee side as well.

kp.k: Client value extends beyond low prices
kp.d: The editorial identifies efficiency, flexibility, expertise and quality as overlapping purchasing criteria. It reports that, in the 2019 Thomson Reuters study, 60 percent or more of corporate respondents who had used ALSPs cited specialized expertise for legal research, regulatory risk and compliance, and litigation and investigation support; expertise was the top driver for each function. The argument concerns matching capabilities to tasks, not simply minimizing rates.
qs: Value to the client is often the primary driver, which includes a metric of cost but is ultimately a more multifaceted calculation.
A service can be expensive and valuable just as it can be cheap and worthless.

When the 2019 study broke this down by function, 60 percent or more of corporate survey respondents who had used ALSPs reported “access to specialized expertise” as a reason for hiring ALSPs for legal research, regulatory risk and compliance, and litigation and investigation support—the top driver for each function.

kp.k: Output-based quality measures support provider selection
kp.d: The editorial argues that credentials, reputation, time spent and subjective judgments are insufficient for meaningful innovation or deciding which traditional practices to retain. Stockton reports that Fidelity uses precision and recall metrics in e-discovery to assess document-review accuracy across providers, internal staff and contractors, informing both internal-versus-external allocation and provider choice. The article also cites research suggesting automated processes are often more accurate for tasks such as e-discovery, without supplying performance figures or study details.
qs: As a result, developing and implementing objective output-based measures of quality is critical.

Stockton notes that Fidelity, for example, has a set of metrics and systems in place pertaining to precision and recall in e-discovery used to determine the accuracy of document review across service providers, internal staff, and contractors.
We use this quantitative measure of quality to understand when a matter should stay in-house versus going to an ALSP and which provider it should go to.

kp.k: Task-based sourcing challenges the traditional provider hierarchy
kp.d: Stockton argues that provider selection should follow the activity and desired outcome: his team still uses law firms for specialized legal advice but considers other providers for repeatable, predictable and data-oriented work. The editorial qualifies the competitive threat to firms through Grasinger's anecdote that a trusted partner's business knowledge and expertise can make a higher hourly rate compatible with a lower total cost and greater confidence in the result.
qs: If we need specialized legal advice, we will always go to a law firm.

But if we’re looking to do any sort of repeatable and predictable work that involves the collection and analysis of data or black-letter-of-the-law legal work, we now have a plethora of other options to choose from.
Higher rate, but likely a much lower total cost, and I can be equally or even more comfortable with the result.

kp.k: Law firms adopt operational models and ALSP partnerships
kp.d: The editorial cites Orrick's Wheeling operations center and Clifford Chance's Best Delivery platform as examples of firms responding to demand for efficiency and flexibility. It reports that Hogan Lovells' February 2018 Elevate partnership provided access to more than 1,500 lawyers. It also discusses the June 2018 LeClairRyan–UnitedLex ULX Partners platform for technology and outsourced support functions, while noting that reports of LeClairRyan's expected dissolution could raise questions about that partnership's merit rather than establishing its success.
qs: Fast-forward to today, and we see law firms outwardly acknowledging their clients’ evolving demands and expectations—including emulating the work and organizational models of ALSPs.
In February 2018, Hogan Lovells announced a partnership with Elevate that provided the law firm with access to the ALSP’s more than 1,500 lawyers.
It is all about being able to respond flexibly to what our clients need.

kp.k: Provider proliferation creates demand for coordination
kp.d: Grasinger suggests that law firms can help clients navigate an increasingly complex provider market, alongside delivering their own expertise. His proposed role depends on knowing the client's business and needs and matching those needs to suitable providers; it also requires substantial client trust. This is a suggested service opportunity, not a demonstrated market-wide business model.
qs: In addition to offering their own expertise, he suggests that law firms can also play a role in helping clients navigate that space.

Now the upshot is that you could be putting a lot of trust in that person, but if you have someone who can know your business, know your needs, and then match what needs you might have to the best options available, then that can be extremely valuable.

kp.k: Rebundling and consolidation remain uncertain future pathways
kp.d: The editorial explicitly leaves unresolved whether ALSPs will develop integrated models resembling or including the Big Four, specialize in discrete tasks, or follow another path. Stockton anticipates consolidation alongside boutique specialization and raises concerns about sustainability, attrition, hiring and career paths. He also questions whether scaled providers could replace some in-house operations capacity, while emphasizing buyers' need to pay for value rather than brand and trust. These are prospective possibilities and concerns, not established outcomes.
qs: Where ALSPs’ collectively rising star goes next is unclear.
It may be that the profession is moving closer to an integration model akin to (and potentially including) the Big Four.
With all this unbundling and provisioning of legal services, the question remains as to who is going to “rebundle” it all.
Do all businesses need in-house operations departments, or can we go to a service provider who may be able to offer more-competitive pricing because they will be able to operate at scale?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The editorial team states that research suggests automated processes are often more accurate for tasks such as e-discovery.
pts.d: This is the document’s closest explicit claim relevant to AI: it concerns automation, without specifying AI technology. It appears within an argument for objective, output-based measures of legal-service quality to inform sourcing decisions. The article primarily discusses ALSPs, legal operations and process redesign; it does not attribute their broader market effects to AI or offer explicit predictions about AI-driven displacement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The automation-accuracy claim rests on linked research; the discussion of quality-based sourcing also draws on Jamal Stockton’s account of Fidelity’s practices.
pts.d: The editorial links to research in the Richmond Journal of Law and Technology but does not report its methods, sample, numerical results or technological scope. Separately, Stockton describes Fidelity’s use of precision and recall to assess document-review accuracy across providers, internal staff and contractors. His account supports the description of quality-based purchasing, rather than independently establishing that automation outperforms human review.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claim describes an existing capability as of the July/August 2019 article, qualified by task and frequency rather than a future deadline.
pts.d: The statement says automated processes are 'often' more accurate for tasks 'like e-discovery'; it does not assert superiority across all legal work. No study period, adoption timetable or future AI-performance forecast is provided. The surrounding discussion makes measurable quality central to deciding where work should be performed.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Corporate legal departments and competing document-review providers are affected through quality-based work-allocation decisions.
pts.d: The identified setting is corporate e-discovery procurement, exemplified by Fidelity. Internal staff, contractors, ALSPs and law firms are compared as possible sources of legal work. The source describes quantitative quality measures informing retention or outsourcing of matters and provider selection; it does not quantify automation-related employment changes or claim benefits for access to justice.
